items.title: You Can Make Custom Concrete Signs This Easily
items.description: Can you make a custom concrete sign using cheap silicone letter and number molds? I wanted to find out. In this build, I use inexpensive silicone molds to cast epoxy numbers, add mica powder and glow pigment, position them inside a simple mold, and then embed them directly into concrete. The result is a surprisingly clean custom address sign that doesn't require expensive equipment or even a 3D printer. This same method could be used for: House numbers Name signs Garden markers Workshop signs Memorial markers Glow-in-the-dark signs Backlit LED signs And both silicone molds I started with cost less than $10. The next experiment might be taking this idea even further and building a concrete sign with illuminated letters. If you enjoy experimental builds, 3D printing, electronics, thrift finds and turning simple materials into useful projects, consider subscribing to Sawdust & Circuits. items.title: Can 3D Printer Filament Fix Motorcycle Body Damage?
items.description: Can 3D printer filament actually repair damaged motorcycle or scooter bodywork? I recently picked up this Honda PCX150, and while I was pretty happy with the purchase at first, the more I looked it over, the more problems I started finding. The rear tire needed replacing, the bodywork had deep scratches from being dropped, and I started wondering if I had paid a little too much. Instead of spending a fortune trying to make it perfect, I decided to see how much I could improve it on a budget. After replacing the rear tire myself, I tackled the damaged plastic panels using something I already had in the shop: ABS 3D printer filament. Using a small butane soldering iron, I melted filament into the deeper scratches, shaped the repairs with nail files and sandpaper, then attempted to match the Honda's pearl white paint using readily available spray paint and mica powder. The goal wasn't a showroom restoration. This was a five-to-ten-foot restoration: make it reliable, make it presentable, and don't spend a fortune doing it. Did the filament repair actually work, and did I manage to turn this questionable scooter purchase back into a decent deal? Let me know what you think in the comments. Would you have bought this PCX150 in the condition I found it? If you enjoy experimental repairs, 3D printing, thrift finds, electronics and unusual shop projects, consider subscribing to Sawdust & Circuits. Thanks for watching, see you next time.

items.title: 9 Must-Have 3D Printing Tools I Actually Use
items.description: What tools actually make 3D printing easier? After more than 10 years of 3D printing, I’ve collected quite a few tools—but some of the most useful ones weren’t even designed for 3D printing. In this video I’m showing the tools I regularly use for trimming, sanding, measuring, cleaning up, modifying, repairing and sometimes even rescuing 3D printed parts. We’ll look at side cutters, nail files, digital calipers, a deburring tool, pin vise and drill bits, super glue, an X-Acto knife, a scraper and one of my favorites—the ultrasonic cutter. Some of these cost only a few dollars, while others are definitely more specialized, but all of them have earned a place near my printers. If you have an unusual tool you use for 3D printing, leave it in the comments. I’m always looking for another excuse to buy a tool. items.title: Gel Blaster Surge Review – BB Volcano or Blaster?
items.description: Today we're testing the Gel Blaster Surge to see if this rechargeable gel blaster is actually a fun backyard toy—or a complete dud. The Surge uses water-grown gellets and features USB Type-C charging, single-shot and full-auto firing modes, plus high- and low-velocity barrels. I also picked up some extra gellets, so naturally we had to grow both types and see if there was any difference. Things got interesting pretty quickly. Instead of consistently firing one gellet at a time, this blaster sometimes shoots one, sometimes two, sometimes three or more—and the velocity seems just as unpredictable. Full-auto works better, although that may just be because eventually statistics are on your side. We'll grow the gellets, compare them, test both firing modes, try the different barrels, and see whether the Gel Blaster Surge is actually worth using. If you own one of these, let me know how yours performs. Does it consistently fire one gellet at a time, or does yours create gellet weather too? Thanks for watching Sawdust and Circuits! #gelblasterguns #GelBlasterSurge #toyreview #SawdustAndCircuits

items.title: Can 3D Printing Save This Broken Klipsch Speaker?
items.description: Can a broken Klipsch Quintet speaker be turned into a completely self-contained Bluetooth speaker? After one of my Klipsch Quintet satellite speakers took a fall, I decided repairing the original enclosure was a little too easy. Instead, I designed a completely new 3D printed enclosure, added a compact mono Bluetooth amplifier, reused the original Klipsch woofer, tweeter and crossover, and turned it into a retro-inspired desktop Bluetooth speaker. Along the way I discovered an interesting piece of old speaker technology hiding behind the woofer: a second magnet originally used for magnetic shielding around CRT televisions. Removing it also gave me the space I needed to fit the crossover inside the new enclosure. I ended up testing two enclosure designs — a sealed version and a ported version — to see which worked better with these small Klipsch drivers. Which version would you build: sealed or ported? And would you have repaired the original speaker or converted it to Bluetooth? Let me know in the comments. If you enjoy 3D printing, electronics, speaker builds, thrift finds and strange workshop experiments, consider subscribing to Sawdust and Circuits. Thanks for watching! #3DPrinting #Klipsch #BluetoothSpeaker #DIYAudio #SawdustAndCircuits

items.title: I Made Invisible Grid Paper… and It Actually Works
items.description: I wanted a portable way to sketch projects on regular paper while still having a grid available when I needed it. The solution turned out to be surprisingly simple: a battery-powered light pad combined with a transparent grid sheet. Put the grid under your paper, turn on the light, and you have instant grid paper. Turn the light off and you're back to a clean drawing with no printed grid lines. In this video I test the setup by sketching one of my recent concrete projects, try drawing with it in a dark room, and talk about a few things I like—and a couple things I would change. The funny part is that the inexpensive transparent grid may actually be my favorite part of the whole setup. Could you use this for woodworking plans, electronics layouts, 3D printing, templates, tracing, or something completely different? Let me know what you would use it for. items.title: I Turned a $1 Thrift Store Ice Tray Into a Concrete Factory
items.description: Yesterday I found a silicone ice cube tray at a thrift store for just $1, so naturally I decided to see if I could turn it into a tiny concrete manufacturing system. In this build I use 3D printing to design a custom insert, create a negative mold, cast that part in two-part silicone, and then use the finished silicone tooling to make repeatable concrete castings. The finished product is, of course, a completely innocent concrete fountain pen holder. Definitely a pen holder. But the bigger experiment is whether 3D printing can be used for more than making finished parts. By using a printer to create masters, molds, jigs, and tooling, one printed design could potentially produce dozens or hundreds of cast products. Can cheap thrift-store finds, 3D printing, silicone, and concrete become a realistic form of small-scale home manufacturing? That’s something I plan to test a lot more. If you enjoy 3D printing, electronics, unusual tools, thrift-store finds, experiments, and DIY builds, consider subscribing to Sawdust & Circuits.

items.title: I Tested the Weird Frequencies You Told Me To Try
items.description: You suggested the frequencies… so today I’m testing them. From 6 Hz and the famous 7.8 Hz Schumann resonance all the way up to 21,000 Hz, we're running through some of the strangest frequency suggestions from the comments. Some are associated online with relaxation, pain relief, tinnitus, the so-called “God frequency,” healing frequencies… and apparently even growing teeth. Yeah. We’re testing that one too. I originally planned to make this a visual experiment using sand, vibration tables, a bass shaker and a 10-inch subwoofer. Unfortunately, the sand had absolutely no interest in cooperating. So we changed plans. In this video we'll test: 6 Hz 7.8 Hz 20 Hz 174 Hz 528 Hz 963 Hz 1,000 Hz 6,111 Hz 21,000 Hz We’ll also talk about what people claim these frequencies do and separate the interesting real science from some of the more questionable internet mythology. Have another strange frequency I should test? Leave the frequency AND what you think it supposedly does in the comments. I may include your suggestion in the next experiment. items.title: Novice vs. Work Sharp: Can I Save This Knife?
items.description: Today’s project starts with ruining a perfectly good knife—and then trying to bring it back. In this video, I test the Work Sharp Original Knife & Tool Sharpener, a compact electric belt sharpening system designed for knives, scissors and other edged tools. Instead of judging sharpness by shaving paper or arm hair, I built a 3D-printed cutting fixture and used a Dillon force gauge to measure how much force each blade needed to cut through fishing line. We begin with a utility razor blade as our baseline, test the knife while dull, damage the edge even further and then see whether a complete sharpening novice can restore it with the Work Sharp. The knife begins at approximately 8.8 newtons, improves to 7 newtons after the first sharpening attempt and eventually reaches an impressive 2.2 newtons. Can a tiny belt sander really make a damaged knife sharper than our razor-blade baseline? items.title: This Phone Mount Has a Refrigerator Built Inside
items.description: Can a tiny refrigerator keep your phone from overheating? In this video, I test a magnetic thermoelectric phone cooler that combines a Peltier module, heatsink, fan, magnetic mount, and—as required by modern technology—RGB lighting. We’ll look at how a Peltier cooler works, watch one through a thermal camera, and compare it with another thermoelectric device: a heat-powered wood-stove fan. Then we’ll attach the cooler to a phone and find out whether it can genuinely reduce temperatures or whether the cold air coming through the car vent is doing most of the work. These coolers may be useful during gaming, wireless charging, GPS navigation, high-resolution video recording, or extremely hot weather—but they also use extra power, create heat on the opposite side, and may introduce condensation under the right conditions. Is this a practical solution for phone overheating or an unnecessarily complicated RGB fan? Let me know what you think in the comments. Thanks for watching, and I’ll see you next time! #phonecooler #PeltierCooler #thermalcamera #SawdustAndCircuits #techreview

items.title: I Tested the “God Frequency” With an Oscilloscope
items.description: Can certain frequencies improve sleep, repair DNA, summon ghosts or even connect you to a higher consciousness? Today on Sawdust & Circuits, I test a Schumann resonance generator using an oscilloscope to see what this strange little wooden box is actually producing. We’ll look at the famous 7.83 Hz Schumann resonance, the 19 Hz “ghost frequency,” 40 Hz brain stimulation, 432 Hz tuning, the 528 Hz “DNA repair” frequency, the 963 Hz “God frequency,” and even the legendary brown note. Some of these frequencies are connected to real science. Others appear to be folklore, spiritual beliefs or very creative marketing. Does the frequency shown on the display match the real output? Does the moving bearing actually react to the selected signal? And is this a useful relaxation device—or just snake oil with a keypad? Watch to the end for the oscilloscope results and my final verdict. What strange frequency should I test next? items.title: I Designed a Bambu AMS Adapter for Small Filament Spools
items.description: Welcome back to **Sawdust and Circuits!** If you've ever tried using small filament spools or sample rolls with the **Bambu Lab AMS**, you've probably run into the same problem—they don't fit like standard spools. Instead of manually respooling every roll, I decided to design my own solution. In this video I design and test a **3D printed small spool adapter** that securely grips smaller filament spools with flexible spring arms, allowing them to feed through the AMS like a standard-sized spool. Along the way I share a bit of my 10-year 3D printing journey—from my first Dremel 3D printer to my current Bambu Lab P1S—and explain why learning CAD has been one of the most valuable skills I've picked up. To test the design, I print a few of my earliest creations using thrift-store filament finds to see if the adapter can reliably handle smaller spools.
